data.text/html:
Gaussian Mixture Models, by hand: watch EM think

An interactive companion to Atif Adib's video "Gaussian Mixture Models Explained | Basics of ML". k-means draws hard borders and assumes round clusters. A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) instead says: every point was produced by one of K bell curves; I just don't know which one. We'll rebuild the video's path: the 1D bell curve, the 2D bell curve, then the Expectation-Maximization (EM) loop, written in plain numpy, which you can step through one E-step and M-step at a time, starting from means you drag into place yourself.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eColor language used throughout.\u003c/strong\u003e Gaussian \u003cstrong\u003e1 = orange\u003c/strong\u003e, \u003cstrong\u003e2 = blue\u003c/strong\u003e, \u003cstrong\u003e3 = green\u003c/strong\u003e, \u003cstrong\u003e4 = amber\u003c/strong\u003e, \u003cstrong\u003e5 = purple\u003c/strong\u003e.\nA point's color is the Gaussian it most likely came from; it fades toward \u003cstrong\u003egray\u003c/strong\u003e the more \u003cem\u003euncertain\u003c/em\u003e that is.\nThe \u003cstrong\u003ered\u003c/strong\u003e curve or marker is always the quantity being measured (a likelihood, a mean you can drag).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
1 · Why not just k-means?

The video opens with the complaint: k-means "cannot handle noise or overlapping clusters and only works really well when the clusters are globular." k-means splits space with straight borders halfway between centroids, so every point gets a hard label and every cluster is implicitly a circle of the same size. A GMM replaces each centroid with a full bell curve (its own center μ, shape Σ and share φ) and replaces hard labels with probabilities. Pick a dataset and compare both, started from identical initial means.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eOn \u003cstrong\u003eelongated\u003c/strong\u003e, k-means cuts the two long stripes \u003cem\u003evertically\u003c/em\u003e (round-cluster assumption). The GMM learns flat, wide ellipses and separates them. Try several seeds.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSwitch to \u003cstrong\u003eoverlapping\u003c/strong\u003e: k-means paints a crisp border, the GMM grays out the contested middle, which is the \u003cem\u003e\"gray out the points it is uncertain about\"\u003c/em\u003e moment from the end of the video.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ebig + small\u003c/strong\u003e: k-means steals points from the big cloud for the small one. Why? (Hint: the border sits halfway between centroids, regardless of spread.)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
2 · The bell curve in 1D

"To describe a bell curve you need two things: its mean μ, around which it is centered, and its variance σ², which describes how sharp or flat it is." Given μ and σ, this equation gives the likelihood of any point x: ||[\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)||]Drag the red triangle (μ), the red circle on the shoulder (σ, sits at μ+σ) and the purple diamond (the point x).

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='Kclp-0' random-id='cc7f416c-9cd8-3ea9-76cc-cbb9622f9968'><marimo-anywidget data-initial-value='{"model_id":"0688d5ab1fb54a368b43ce7c66dbd20a"}' data-label='null' data-model-id='"0688d5ab1fb54a368b43ce7c66dbd20a"'></marimo-anywidget></marimo-ui-element>
Python agrees with the widget: the point sits 1.50 σ from μ, so its likelihood is e^(−z²/2) = 0.325 times the peak.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag x onto μ: the likelihood is the maximum, \u003cem\u003e\"the closer you sample from the mean the higher the likelihood.\"\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePut x at exactly μ+σ, then μ+2σ: relative height is always \u003cstrong\u003e60.7 %\u003c/strong\u003e and \u003cstrong\u003e13.5 %\u003c/strong\u003e, whatever σ is.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eHalve σ with the shoulder handle: the peak \u003cstrong\u003edoubles\u003c/strong\u003e (the area must stay 1). A likelihood is a density, so it can exceed 1. Try σ = 0.25.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3 · The bell curve in 2D

"The mean would be represented by a vector, with one mean for each dimension, and sigma by a matrix containing pairwise variances. The equation remains the same, except simple multiplications are replaced by matrix multiplications." ||[\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}\mid\boldsymbol\mu,\Sigma) = \frac{1}{2\pi\,|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)\Big), \qquad \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_x^2 & \rho\,\sigma_x\sigma_y\\ \rho\,\sigma_x\sigma_y & \sigma_y^2\end{pmatrix}||]Compare to 1D: ||((x-\mu)^2/\sigma^2||) became ||((\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)||), the squared Mahalanobis distance. The off-diagonal term ρ is what lets a GMM learn tilted ellipses, which k-means can't.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet ρ = 0: the ellipse aligns with the axes and Σ is diagonal. Set σx = σy too: a circle, the only shape k-means \"believes in\".\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePut the ◆ at (1.5, 1.5) and then at (1.5, −1.5) with ρ = 0.8. Same Euclidean distance, very different likelihood: the Mahalanobis distance follows the ellipse.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePush ρ toward ±0.95 and watch |Σ| shrink toward 0: the bell collapses onto a line and its peak shoots up.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Expectation-Maximization, one step at a time

"Just like any other clustering algorithm, GMM is iterative and has two steps." With K Gaussians, mixing weights φ_k (the video's Phi), means μ_k and covariances Σ_k: E-step (assignment / "expectation"). For every point, compute its likelihood under each Gaussian, then "convert these likelihoods to weights by dividing each likelihood vector by its sum": ||[w_{ik} = \frac{\varphi_k\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\varphi_j\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}||]M-step (update / "maximization"). Re-fit each Gaussian to all points, weighted by ||(w_{ik}||): ||[N_k=\sum_i w_{ik},\quad \varphi_k=\frac{N_k}{n},\quad \boldsymbol\mu_k=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_i w_{ik}\mathbf{x}_i,\quad \Sigma_k=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_i w_{ik}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k)(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k)^\top||]Repeat. The log-likelihood ||(\log L=\sum_i\log\sum_k\varphi_k\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_k,\Sigma_k)||) never goes down. The e_step / m_step / run_em functions in the first code cell are exactly these formulas in numpy (the video uses scipy.stats.multivariate_normal; here the density is written out with a Cholesky factor). Step 1: like k-means, "we randomly initialize our Gaussians". Here you are the random initializer: drag the colored means (each starts as a circle with Σ = I and φ = 1/K) anywhere, even somewhere silly.

Set K = 1: EM converges in one step (it's just the sample mean and covariance).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · Soft assignments: graying out the doubt

The video's punchline: the model "is not only able to cluster the points but also gray out the points it is uncertain about, as they are equally likely to have come from either of the two Gaussians." That uncertainty is just the final weight row ||(w_{i\cdot}||), the video's predict_proba: likelihoods times Phi, divided by their sum. Below, using the converged model from section 4, every point whose top weight is below the threshold is grayed out.

The gray points form a \u003cem\u003ecurved\u003c/em\u003e band (a quadratic boundary), not k-means' straight line, because the two Σ differ.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Sandbox: generate a mixture, fit a mixture

Build a hidden mixture of true K random Gaussians, then fit a GMM with your own fit K. The bar chart on the right fits every K from 1 to 6 and scores it with the BIC ||(=-2\log L + p\log n||) with ||(p = 6K-1||) free parameters in 2D. Lowest BIC wins, which is a standard way to pick K when you don't know it.

What do the clusters look like? (Usually two overlap almost completely.)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003ccode\u003efit K\u003c/code\u003e = true K and change only \u003ccode\u003einit seed\u003c/code\u003e. Does the final log-likelihood change? EM only finds a \u003cstrong\u003elocal\u003c/strong\u003e maximum, so production code runs several restarts.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePush \u003ccode\u003efit K\u003c/code\u003e to 6 with n = 60. Watch for a tiny, needle-thin ellipse: a Gaussian collapsing onto a few points sends the likelihood toward +∞ (the reason for the \u003ccode\u003ereg\u003c/code\u003e term in \u003ccode\u003em_step\u003c/code\u003e).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>
